title: The Impact of Peer Feedback on Chinese EFL Junior High School Students’ Writing Performance
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether adding peer feedback to standard teacher feedback improves writing performance and writing self-efficacy for Chinese EFL students. The problem motivating the study is that junior high school students in China often receive delayed, generalized teacher feedback, focus mainly on scores, and show weak motivation and confidence in writing. The authors ask whether peer feedback can better support writing ability—especially content, organization, and grammar—and self-efficacy dimensions of motivation and confidence.

The intervention compared two intact grade 9 classes in a Chinese public junior high school over 8 weeks. The experimental class received both teacher feedback and peer feedback; students commented on, discussed, and revised peers’ writing using standards focused on content, organization, and grammar. The control class received teacher feedback only, representing the baseline/comparator condition in this study. Writing ability was measured with pre- and post-tests scored by two experienced teachers, and self-efficacy was examined through post-intervention questionnaires.

The population consisted of 100 ninth-grade students (50 experimental, 50 control), ages 13-16, in one public school in China. The setting was a regular classroom writing instruction context rather than a lab or online environment. The study used convenience sampling with intact classes, so the comparison was non-randomized.

The main conclusion is that combining peer feedback with teacher feedback produced larger gains in overall writing scores than teacher feedback alone. The authors report stronger improvement for the experimental group in content and organization, with smaller gains in grammar; for the teacher-feedback-only group, gains were smaller overall. Questionnaire results also suggested that students viewed peer feedback more positively than teacher feedback alone and perceived it as more helpful for motivation and confidence. Overall, the paper presents peer-plus-teacher feedback as a stronger alternative to teacher-only feedback for secondary EFL writing, though the evidence is limited to one short-term, single-site study.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental study with a comparison group, pre/post testing, and clear sample/reporting, but it uses convenience intact classes rather than random assignment and does not report standardized effect sizes or stronger controls for bias.
impact_tier_rationale: The study shows modest positive impacts for a priority writing-learning population, with a statistically significant posttest advantage and clear gains in content and organization, but effect sizes are not reported and results are from a single junior high EFL setting rather than broad high school samples.

finding.finding_summary: In a quasi-experiment with 100 Chinese grade 9 EFL students (experimental n=50; control n=50), the class receiving peer feedback in addition to teacher feedback outperformed the teacher-feedback-only class on overall writing posttest scores after 8 weeks. Mean writing scores rose from 9.48 to 10.98 in the experimental group versus 9.52 to 9.92 in the control group; the between-group posttest difference was 1.06 points (p=.007). Sub-analytic results showed significantly larger gains for content (MD=0.64, p<.001) and organization (MD=0.38, p=.010), while grammar showed no significant between-group posttest difference (MD=0.04, p=.785), though within-group grammar improved in both groups.
finding.measure: Timed EFL writing pre/post tests scored by two experienced teachers on overall writing and analytic traits: content, organization, grammar

finding.finding_summary: Survey results after the 8-week intervention suggested more favorable self-efficacy, motivation, and confidence in the peer-feedback-plus-teacher-feedback class than in the teacher-feedback-only class. For example, 80-82% of experimental students agreed or strongly agreed that peer feedback improved motivation/confidence, compared with about 58-62% of control students reporting similar benefits from teacher feedback; across specific motivation items, experimental endorsement was typically 76-82%, versus roughly 48-60% in control, and confidence items were typically 70-82% versus 52-62%.
finding.measure: Post-intervention Likert questionnaire on writing self-efficacy, motivation, confidence, and attitudes toward feedback

finding.finding_summary: The peer-feedback condition appeared to support discussion, consideration of others' suggestions, and peer-based review behaviors that align with collaboration and reflective revision processes. Descriptively, 76-82% of students in the experimental class agreed or strongly agreed that peer feedback improved their motivation to let peers read their writing, read peers' writing, discuss peers' writing, and consider peer suggestions, exceeding the teacher-feedback-only class on parallel items.
finding.measure: Student self-report questionnaire items on discussion, peer reading, and considering suggestions
